<|channel|>analysis<|message|>We need to answer "Why did Susan forgive her husband after he had an affair, and of course she forgave him?" That's asking: after Matthew had an affair, Susan forgave him. The question asks why she forgave him, what was the reason? Options:

A. She believes that her husband's infidelity, Myra Jenkins, will not pose a threat to her marriage

B. She is trying to rationalize the reality that she cannot accept

C. For it was inevitable that the handsome, blond, attractive, manly man, Matthew Rawlings, should be at times tempted

D. Because she doesn't think this matter is very serious

We need to choose which is best supported by the text.

We need to recall what the text says: When Matthew had the affair, Susan "forgave him, of course." Then: "Except that forgiveness is hardly the word. Understanding, yes. But if you understand something, you don’t forgive it, you are the thing itself: forgiveness is for what you don’t understand. Nor had he confessed—what sort of word is that?" The text: "The whole thing was not important. After all, years ago they had joked: Of course I’m not going to be faithful to you, no one can be faithful to one other person for a whole lifetime." But after the affair, Susan had irritable emotions but didn't hold a lot of resentment. She says the affair didn't represent a serious threat to marriage and could be tolerated. The text suggests they had developed a pattern of rationalising fidelity as low expectation. The raw text: "They had avoided the pitfall so many of their friends had fallen into—of buying a house in the country for the sake of the children ... They looked around them, and took lessons... They were not going to make the same mistakes." Later: "The whole thing was not important. After all, years ago they had joked..." The text indicates Susan laughs off the affair and forgives. She was rationalizing that infidelity is inevitable and so not significant. She sees it's not a threat to the marriage: "she could hardly be expected to be proud of the newspaper... They had avoided the pitfalls..." She is aware that Matthew would want to sometimes be tempted, but can't rectify her own.

Also later: "Surely not the forgiveness... Salem." "But if you understand something, you don’t forgive it...  The whole thing was not important." The narrative suggests she wanted to rationalize, forgiving because it's not serious, as she and Matthew had accepted imperfection. The answer: maybe option B or D. Option A says she believes infidelity won't threaten marriage. Option C says it's inevitable. Option D says she doesn't think it's serious. The text: "She forgave him, of course. Except that forgiveness is hardly the word. Understanding, yes. But if you understand something, you don’t forgive it, you are the thing itself: forgiveness is for what you don’t understand. Nor had he confessed—what sort of word is that?" She rationalizes: "The whole thing was not important." She likely sees it's not that serious but may rationalize why it's inevitable.

Option C: "For it was inevitable that the handsome, blond, attractive, manly man, Matthew Rawlings, should be at times tempted." She seems to think it's inevitable. That is indeed in the text: "It was inevitable that the handsome, blond, attractive, manly man, Matthew Rawlings, should be at times tempted." That phrase appears in about halfway. The line: "But in the text at 'Seeing Susan had no matte.'" Actually check the passage: "It was inevitable that the handsome, blond, attractive, manly man, Matthew Rawlings, should be at times tempted (oh, what a word!) by the attractive girls at parties she could not attend because of the four children...". So they include the phrase that it's inevitable. The question: Why did Susan forgive? That answer fits option C: because she believed it was inevitable. But also the text says "The whole thing was not important... She would have to take lessons." Possibly they see it as inevitable and not threatening.

Option A: She believes infidelity will not pose a threat. That's also plausible. But the text emphasises "It was inevitable that Matthew should be tempted" and she apparently "does not feel the affair as big". It mentions forgiveness is not typical but "It was inevitable." So the best answer: C.

But check the phrasing: "Why did Susan forgive her husband after he had an affair, and of course she forgave him?" The correct answer: She rationalised that fidelity was unrealistic, so the affair was inevitable and not threatening to marriage. Which matches option C.

Option D: Because she doesn't think this matter is very serious. That's also plausible but one is quite murky. But the best choice: C.

Thus answer: \boxed{C}.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>\boxed{C}
